kp.k: Reliance concerns delegated cognitive work, not merely output adoption
kp.d: This May 2026 arXiv preprint develops a process-oriented measure in AI-assisted programming, rather than studying legal work directly. The authors argue that output acceptance and self-reported reliance inadequately describe multi-turn workflows: similar final outputs can conceal different allocations of planning, execution and verification between users and AI. Their focus is cognitive processes and understanding, not simply artifact quality.
qs: In this work, we instead characterize reliance by how cognitive work is distributed between the user and the AI tool, i.e. how many of the planning, execution, and verification steps that a user would otherwise perform are offloaded to the AI.

Intuitively, a user who asks the tool to solve an entire coding task is more reliant than one who decomposes the task, queries the model for subcomponents, and verifies each step, even if both produce similar final outputs (Figure 1 (A)).

kp.k: Offloading score estimates steps saved against simulated human workflows
kp.d: The metric replaces each AI-assisted step with a simulated human-only sequence accomplishing the same sub-goal. With n observed steps and m counterfactual steps, the score is (m−n)/m, generally ranging between 0 and 1. It approximates cognitive effort through step counts rather than measuring effort directly. Counterfactuals represent an average user, not the individual participant. The pipeline uses recorded screenshots, clicks and keystrokes, gpt-5.1 for workflow induction, and gpt-5.2 for counterfactual generation and descriptive labels.
qs: Since cognitive effort is not directly observable from the final artifacts or tool usage alone, we estimate how each AI-assisted sub-goal would have been completed without the tool.
Typically, m ≥ n, reflecting the additional work required without the tool.
This fraction, referred to as offloading score, serves as the primary scalar measure of reliance in empirical evaluation.

kp.k: Time pressure distinguishes offloading score from baseline measures
kp.d: The between-subjects study included 40 U.S.-based Upwork developers familiar with AI coding tools, completing four web-application tasks: five participants per task per condition, with 1-hour versus 4-hour limits. Offloading scores averaged 0.451 in the short condition versus 0.308 in the long condition (p = 0.018); the abstract describes the increase as +43%. Baselines did not significantly distinguish conditions at the 5% level, including AI-code fraction (0.152 versus 0.052, p = 0.072) and self-reported cognitive load (3.63 versus 3.56, p = 0.881). The authors treat the expected association between time pressure and reliance as a validation criterion, not a gold-standard direct measurement of reliance.
qs: We introduce two experimental conditions that vary time constraints, a short condition (1 hour) and a long condition (4 hours).
Each task is completed by 5 participants per condition, resulting in n = 20 participants per condition.
From Figure 4, we observe that none of the baseline metrics show significant differences between conditions at the 5% level, while offloading score is able to do so.

kp.k: Time pressure shifts users toward delegation and direct reuse
kp.d: Descriptive labels show more execution-oriented interactions under short limits (38.5% versus 29.6%) and more direct reuse of outputs (25.6% versus 11.9%). Long-condition users more frequently rejected outputs (22.8% versus 15.6%) and used AI for planning (39.8% versus 33.3%). These are descriptive behavioral findings accompanying the primary metric, not separately established causal mechanisms. Appendix B reports similar absolute AI-assisted step counts but a higher AI-assisted proportion under short limits: 16.40% versus 9.68%, p = 0.03.
qs: Higher reliance manifests as increased delegation and more direct reuse of outputs from the tool.

In contrast, users in the long condition reject outputs more often (22.8% vs. 15.6% in short) and use the model more for planning-related processes (39.8% vs. 33.3%), indicating more selective engagement and greater user agency.

kp.k: Intrinsic tests support plausibility, sensitivity and stability
kp.d: Twenty randomly sampled users rated five counterfactual steps from their own workflows. The main text reports over 85% rated plausible at ≥3 on a five-point scale. Counterfactuals were also semantically closer to recorded human workflows for the same task than other tasks in a four-task dataset (Wilcoxon p ≈ 10−6; permutation p < 10−4). Replacing 5%, 10% and 20% of AI-assisted steps with human-only alternatives reduced mean scores by 6.9%, 9.0% and 12.9%, respectively; the authors report stability across model, reasoning-effort and paraphrasing variations. gpt-5.2 agreed with human labels on 80% of cognitive-process and 81% of output-use annotations.
qs: We ask 20 randomly sampled users to evaluate 5 counterfactual steps from their own workflows.
Mean values fell in the 5%, 10%, and 20% replacement conditions by 6.9%, 9.0%, and 12.9%.
These decreases were significant at the 5% level under both paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for all three levels, indicating that the metric is sensitive to true reductions in AI usage.

kp.k: Appropriate reliance depends on the outcome being protected
kp.d: The authors argue that reliance becomes inappropriate relative to a normative goal, rather than at a universally unacceptable score. They illustrate this with code understanding, measured through ten implementation questions scored 0, 0.33, 0.67 or 1.00 and averaged for each user. They choose 0.33 as an illustrative sufficient-understanding threshold, while acknowledging that productivity and understanding may require different standards. Section 5 identifies gpt-5.2 as the recall evaluator, whereas Appendix E.5 describes gpt-5-mini evaluating retrieved evidence from each participant’s submitted repository.
qs: However, such normative judgments have to be made based on the user goal, or what constitutes undesirable outcomes of inappropriate reliance.
To illustrate defining appropriate reliance, we use a threshold of 0.33 (partially correct) as an indicator of “good enough understanding”.

In practice, it is possible that the normative standards for different goals (e.g., what is the right reliance for harnessing productivity gain versus maintaining a good understanding) will differ, and one needs to make a priority judgment.

kp.k: Understanding associations strengthen only after excluding a high-recall cluster
kp.d: Section 5 reports a negative association of −0.145 between offloading and system recall, versus −0.101 for the strongest baseline; Figure 16 describes its outcome as binary recall ≥0.33. Excluding a moderate-to-high-reliance, high-recall cluster increases the reported Pearson correlation to −0.440. For the remaining users, the authors propose an illustrative offloading threshold of 0.33 associated with recall below 0.33. This threshold arises from the study’s subgroup analysis; the document does not establish a universal threshold or longitudinal skill-loss effect.
qs: When excluding users in the outlier cluster (30% of users in the green region in Figure 6, to be discussed below), we find that the Pearson correlation of offloading score and system recall increases to −0.440.

For these users, we can define overreliance as the reliance level that leads to an undesirable level of system recall of below 0.33, setting a threshold for overreliance as offloading score = 0.33 as shown in Figure 6.

kp.k: High reliance can coexist with learning and retained understanding
kp.d: In the high-reliance, high-recall cluster, five of eleven users reported using AI for features they could not implement independently. One interviewee described iterative planning to explore alternatives. The authors interpret this as suggesting that substantial reliance can be appropriate when AI supports learning; the highest score in this cluster was 0.65 with sufficient understanding retained. Six follow-up interviews also suggest that habit and speed can accompany low understanding, while low reliance can reflect limited knowledge of tool capabilities. The authors explicitly characterize interview evidence as anecdotal rather than representative.
qs: This distinct pattern suggests that the normative standard of appropriate reliance should be set differently for these users: when the tool is used for learning, high reliance is often still appropriate for desirable outcomes.

Our experiment does not provide enough data to identify the threshold for inappropriate reliance in this condition: the highest offloading score in this cluster is 0.65, and the user still maintained a good enough understanding.
We provide these interview findings as anecdotal qualitative context for the quantitative patterns observed across users, and are not necessarily representative of the full participant pool.

kp.k: Reliance relates to ownership more than reported trust
kp.d: Additional analyses report correlations of +0.23 with perceived distribution of cognitive work, −0.37 with perceived project ownership, and −0.07 with trust. Trust was high overall: 35 of 40 participants rated it between 4 and 5. The authors found no clear tool-specific reliance pattern at this sample size; users of the most common tools, Claude and ChatGPT, exhibited wide variation. These are sample-level associations, not evidence that ownership or a particular product causes reliance.
qs: We find that offloading score is positively correlated with the perceived distribution of cognitive work between the user and tool (+0.23) and negatively correlated with perceived ownership of the project (−0.37), providing corroborating evidence for validating the metric.
In general, we don’t find a clear pattern of a single tool leading to higher or lower reliance.

kp.k: Measurement limitations constrain generalization and proposed future applications
kp.d: The authors acknowledge validation against only one behavioral driver, 40 programming participants, imperfect workflow induction, potentially unrealistic counterfactuals and unequal applicability of average-user simulations across skill levels. Step counts may miss unobservable cognition. They propose future personalized estimates for user reflection and use of the score as an agent-training signal to mitigate overreliance; these are prospective applications, not tested interventions or demonstrated findings about legal services.
qs: Errors in this estimation directly affect the metric.
More broadly, our formulation assumes that cognitive effort can be approximated through workflow steps, which may not capture all aspects that are not externally observable.
We acknowledge the large variance in user skill level and habits might mean that the general counterfactual is not equally applicable.
Offloading Score can also serve as a signal for training agents that actively mitigate overreliance by encouraging more balanced interaction patterns.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Padmakumar and co-authors claim that AI changes the allocation of cognitive work in programming, with time pressure associated with greater delegation and more direct reuse of AI outputs. Their proposed offloading score measures these changes more sensitively than the tested baseline measures.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about AI-assisted programming, not legal services. The authors define offloading score as (m−n)/m, where n is the observed workflow length and m is the estimated human-only counterfactual length. They treat saved workflow steps as a proxy for cognitive effort offloaded, rather than measuring cognition or productivity directly. They report higher offloading under a one-hour deadline than a four-hour deadline, accompanied by more execution-oriented requests and direct output reuse. They also report a generally negative relationship between reliance and code understanding, but identify users who maintained understanding despite substantial reliance, suggesting that AI used for learning can augment capabilities without the same observed understanding deficit. Proposed future applications include user reflection, personalized reliance estimates and training agents to mitigate overreliance.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest principally on a controlled study of 40 experienced freelance developers, supplemented by metric-validation exercises, post-task surveys and six follow-up interviews.
pts.d: Participants completed four web-development tasks, with 20 participants in each deadline condition. Reported mean offloading scores were 0.451 under the short deadline and 0.308 under the long deadline (p = 0.018); the abstract describes the difference as +43%. None of the tested usage-based or cognitive-load baselines distinguished conditions at the 5% significance level. Short-condition interactions were more execution-oriented (38.5% versus 29.6%) and more often involved direct reuse (25.6% versus 11.9%). The authors report a negative association with system recall of −0.145, increasing in magnitude to −0.440 after excluding a high-reliance, high-recall cluster; Figure 16 describes its outcome as recall dichotomized at 0.33. Understanding was assessed through ten implementation questions scored by an LLM against code evidence, with the main text and appendix naming different judging models. Counterfactual validation included participant plausibility ratings, semantic comparisons with recorded human workflows and sensitivity/stability tests. Descriptive labels achieved reported model–human agreement of 80% and 81%. Interviews supplied anecdotal explanations: some low-recall users delegated for speed or habit and did not verify implementation, while some high-recall users used AI to explore unfamiliar work. These observations do not constitute a longitudinal test of deskilling or a tested intervention to reduce overreliance.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The empirical findings concern short programming sessions reported in a May 2026 preprint; longer-term cognitive effects and agent-design applications remain motivations or future possibilities.
pts.d: The experiment contrasts one-hour and four-hour task limits using participants’ chosen AI tools. Appropriateness is explicitly conditional on the desired outcome: preserving code understanding may imply a different reliance standard from maximizing productivity. The authors illustrate a recall threshold of 0.33 and an offloading threshold of 0.33 after excluding the high-recall cluster, rather than establishing a universal boundary. They cannot identify an inappropriate-reliance threshold for the learning-oriented cluster, whose highest observed score was 0.65 with adequate understanding. They acknowledge that validation uses only one reference variable, that the small programming sample may not generalize, and that simulated average-user counterfactuals, imperfect workflow induction and step granularity constrain the measure. No date is specified for personalized measurement or agents that mitigate overreliance.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is U.S.-based freelance developers familiar with AI coding tools; proposed beneficiaries are AI users and agent designers.
pts.d: For developers, the reported changes concern delegation of planning, execution and verification work; selective engagement with generated outputs; understanding of the resulting code; and perceived ownership. Higher offloading correlated negatively with perceived ownership (−0.37). The authors distinguish users who delegate familiar work for speed or habit, users who learn unfamiliar features through AI interaction, and lower-reliance users whose limited awareness of tool capabilities may constrain use. They find no clear tool-specific reliance pattern in this sample and emphasize variation among users of the same tools. The proposed measurement framework could help users reflect on reliance and designers build mitigating interventions, but these benefits are not demonstrated through intervention trials. No findings are offered about lawyers, legal clients, law firms, legal markets or access to justice.
